extracted.intended_audience: novelists, students of fiction, and serious creative writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and executing narrative method (point of view, pictorial vs dramatic treatment), pacing, preparation of climax, scene-making, and character-rendering in the writing of long fiction (novels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lay up the climax in the opening picture / economy of preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The climax of the story... is laid up betimes in the descriptive picture.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare and accumulate reserves of effect early (in description/picture) so the climax has only the final touch to perform. Examples: Balzac places descriptive material early in Eugénie Grandet and La Recherche de l'Absolu so the slow ruin/climax can be shown by progressive destruction rather than by new incidents. Anti-pattern: delaying preparation until the climax or trying to supply all necessary force at the moment of climax (which produces strain and exaggerated stress).

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax should complete and add the touch that makes the book whole
rubrics_metrics.description: “The climax ought to complete, to add the touch that makes the book whole and organic; that is its task, and that only.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the climax to fulfil the intention already implicit in the work rather than to introduce new burdens. Avoid distracting the climax with unresolved material that could have been dispatched earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hinging climax on a sudden discovery when the effect is gradual
rubrics_metrics.description: “The worst kind of disappointment does not happen like that, falling as a stroke; it steals into a life and spreads imperceptibly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the subject demands a slow change (decay, disillusionment), present the climax as a gradual, pictorial impression rather than as a single dramatic revelation. Anti-pattern: resolving a long emotional process with a single contrived disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy — save force from deliberate expatiation
rubrics_metrics.description: “He saves his climax... from the burden of deliberate expatiation... leaves nothing for it to accomplish but just the necessary touch.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overwriting or over-explaining at the point of climactic effect. Keep the climactic passage free to perform its final function by handling preparatory material earlier and subtly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterate a single effect with growing intensity where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: “Reiterating one effect with growing intensity—always at the pitch of high hope and sharp disappointment, always prepared to heighten and sharpen it a little further.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For subjects built on obsession or escalating ruin, structure the narrative as a sustained, intensifying repetition rather than a varied series of unrelated incidents. Example: Claes in La Recherche de l'Absolu—each experiment raises hope and then disappointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting and accumulation of visible loss to externalize internal decline
rubrics_metrics.description: “The disappearance is the outward sign of his own personal surrender to his idea... the spreading devastation around him... spreads through his pictures and treasures to his family.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a richly rendered world early so its progressive denudation can visually track a character’s collapse. Create tangible, successive losses that renew rather than dilute the effect of repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art of preparation should be unobtrusive — unrecognizable until attained
rubrics_metrics.description: “The art of preparation is no art if it betrays itself at the outset... By definition it is unrecognizable until it attains its end; it is the art of rendering an impression that is found to have been made, later on, but that evades detection at the moment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare the reader without calling attention to the preparation. If the reader notices the author’s planning, the effect is spoiled. Aim for invisible structural work that rewards retrospective recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view governs method — decide narrator's relation to the story
rubrics_metrics.description: “The whole intricate question of method... is governed by the question of the point of view—the question of the relation in which the narrator stands to the story.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the narrator (omniscient, a spokesman in the book, or the authorial voice) with reference to what the subject requires: whether it needs a dramatic immediacy, a pictorial perspective, or a probe into consciousness. The chosen point of view determines allowable techniques and the shape of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize the author by bringing a spokesman into the book when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the storyteller is in the story himself, the author is dramatized; his assertions gain in weight, for they are backed by the presence of the narrator in the pictured scene.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When trust in the authorial voice is weak or arbitrary assertion would be problematic, create a narrator-character within the fiction whose perspective legitimates claims and supplies a contained point of view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer objective presentation (showing) for explorations of consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: “Far better it would be to see him while his mind is actually at work in the agitation... The matter would then be objective and visible to the reader.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the narrative must explore a mind deeply, favor scenes that let the reader witness mental activity in the moment (dramatic enactment, interior scenes) rather than relying solely on retrospective report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match method to subject: dramatic form vs pictorial/retrospective form
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dramatic, strictly scenic form for stories that can be revealed through action and episode. Use pictorial/retrospective narration for wide-ranging subjects, character studies, or works that require panoramic survey and accumulated impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand limitations of strict drama: restricted access to private mind
rubrics_metrics.description: “In rigid drama of this kind there is naturally no admission of the reader into the private mind of any of the characters; their thoughts and motives are transmuted into action.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept the sacrifices of strictly scenic drama: compactness and objectivity at the expense of interior penetration. Choose this form only when the loss of direct psychological access is acceptable or desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictorial narration for large-scale, panoramic, or soul-studying subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: “Wherever the story is too big, too comprehensive, too widely ranging, to be treated scenically... these stories... we regard as rather pictorial than dramatic—meaning that they call for some narrator, somebody who knows, to contemplate the facts and create an impression of them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For novels that span many lives, long time, or deep psychological growth, use an organizing consciousness (authorial or a character-narrator) to gather, fuse, and present the accumulated material coherently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed methods are legitimate — enter consciousness within a scenic plan
rubrics_metrics.description: “The method of execution is much looser... he allows himself as much freedom as he pleases... he never hesitates to lay bare the mind of any of his people, at any moment, if it seems to help the force or the lucidity of the scene.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to combine scenic/dramatic scenes with moments of interior revelation or retrospective commentary, provided the combination serves clarity and effect. Tolstoy’s mixed method illustrates how to follow chronology scenically while entering consciousness as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure sufficient preparation/condensation when a crisis must occur early
rubrics_metrics.description: “If, therefore, the situation is to be really made and constituted, the space it may cover must be tightly packed; the method should be that which most condenses and concentrates the representation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a story’s inciting crisis must appear early (as in Anna Karenina), compress and concentrate the preparatory material so the reader can grasp the character’s history and motives before high emotion occurs. Anti-pattern: scenic immediacy without condensed background leading to perceived arbitrariness of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render characters enough from within before subjecting them to extreme emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: “She must be represented upon such a critical height of emotion before there is time, by Tolstoy’s method, to create the right effect for her... She has not yet become a presence familiar enough.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give characters sufficient inner life and context (by scene, memory, or concentrated portrait) before expecting readers to accept them at peaks of passion or decisive choice. Otherwise their actions will feel unearned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small scenic glimpses to enrich character and accelerate the story
rubrics_metrics.description: “The half-page is not a diversion or an interlude; it speeds the story by augmenting the tone and the value of the lives that we are watching.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, vivid scenes or fleeting images can add depth to characters and reinforce the narrative tone without detouring from forward motion. Employ such micro-scenes to make characters feel fuller and to contribute to eventual climactic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inconsistency of method — do not shift point of view arbitrarily
rubrics_metrics.description: “To glance upon the story from a height and to give a general impression of its course—this is at once to remove the point of view from the reader and to set up a new one somewhere else; the method is no longer consistent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a coherent relation between narrator and story. Shifting between scenic immediacy and retrospective generalization can be powerful but risks incoherence if done without clear purpose. Make methodical shifts deliberate and justified by subject demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designer’s pleasure: craft strokes that the critic and reader can perceive
rubrics_metrics.description: “The novelist makes the stroke, but the critic makes it again by perceiving it, and is legitimately satisfied by the sense of having perceived it with good artistry.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose narrative effects (preparations, withheld details, structural strokes) so that perceptive readers recover and appreciate the artistry in hindsight. Aim for structural elegance that rewards recognition rather than obvious manipulation.
